usage: 안 (inner) + 방 (room, 房); the biggest/main bedroom, traditionally the household head's room
차지하다 = to take/occupy; the natural verb when someone grabs the best room
an attached bathroom is a big selling point, so this phrase shows up in listings
the standard pair Koreans use to divide bedrooms among family or roommates
examples: 여기가 안방이에요.
This is the master bedroom.
Pointing it out on a flat tour; 여기가 X-이에요 is the bare 'this is X' frame
저는 안방 쓰고, 동생은 작은방 써요.
I use the master bedroom and my younger sibling uses the small room.
쓰다 ('use') is the everyday verb for occupying a room, not 살다
집 보러 갔는데 안방이 생각보다 넓더라고요.
I went to see the place and the master bedroom was bigger than I'd expected.
-더라고요 reports something you personally noticed on the spot, perfect for a viewing
nuance: 안방 is literally 안 ('inner') + 방 ('room', from the hanja 房), so it points not to size first but to the 'innermost, main' bedroom — culturally the room of the household head, historically where the senior couple slept. The near-synonym trap is 큰방: 큰방 just means 'the big room' by floor area, while 안방 carries the 'master / main' status even in a flat where it isn't literally the largest. Don't confuse it with 거실 (the shared living room) — 안방 is private sleeping space. English speakers often over-extend it and call every bedroom 안방; only the one main room is 안방, the rest are 작은방 or plain 방. It pairs naturally with 안방 화장실 (en-suite) and the contrast set 안방 vs 작은방 when splitting rooms.

mistakes: Calling any bedroom 안방. WHY: 안방 specifically means the one main/master room; the others are 작은방 or 방. FIX: reserve 안방 for the principal bedroom only.
Confusing 안방 with 거실 (living room). WHY: they look similar to a beginner but 안방 is a private bedroom while 거실 is the shared lounge. FIX: use 거실 for the open family area, 안방 for the couple's room.
Saying 큰방 when you mean the 'master' room. WHY: 큰방 only describes size, not status. FIX: use 안방 when you mean the main bedroom regardless of which is physically biggest.

usage: 다용도 多用途 ('many-use', i.e. multi-purpose) + 실 室 ('room'); the back room off the kitchen
to keep (it) in the utility room
두다 = to keep/store; what you do with the washer, kimchi fridge, bulky stuff
to have a separate utility room
따로 있다 = to exist separately; a common plus point in a listing
정리 整理 = sorting out; it clutters fast, so this is a recurring chore
examples: 세탁기는 다용도실에 있어요.
The washing machine is in the utility room.
Basic location sentence; 에 marks where a thing sits
김치냉장고는 다용도실에 둬요.
We keep the kimchi fridge in the utility room.
두다 ('keep/store') is the habitual-storage verb, more natural here than 있다
이 집은 다용도실이 따로 있어서 마음에 들어요.
I like this place because it has a separate utility room.
다용도실이 따로 있다 is the set phrase house-hunters use as a selling point
nuance: 다용도실 is a Sino-Korean compound: 다용도 多用途 literally 'many + use + purpose' = multi-purpose, plus 실 室 'room'. It's the small enclosed back space off the kitchen (often behind the 베란다) where the washing machine, 김치냉장고, cleaning supplies and recycling live — a near-universal feature of Korean apartments. The synonym to keep apart is 창고 倉庫 ('storehouse'): a 창고 is dead storage, while a 다용도실 is an active work-and-store space you use daily. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't assume laundry happens in the bathroom as in many Western homes — in Korea the washer lives in the 다용도실 (or 베란다); second, don't translate it as 'laundry room', because it does far more than laundry. It collocates with 세탁기, 김치냉장고, and 따로 있다.

Calling it 창고 (storehouse). WHY: 창고 is passive dead storage; 다용도실 is an active, in-home utility space. FIX: use 다용도실 for the working back room, 창고 for a true storeroom.
Rendering it 'laundry room'. WHY: it handles storage, the kimchi fridge and recycling too, not just laundry. FIX: say 'utility room' and let 세탁실 be the narrow 'laundry-only' term.

usage: 신발 (shoes) + 장 (cabinet, 欌); the built-in cabinet at the 현관 where shoes are stored
to put into the shoe cabinet
넣다 = to put inside; the action right after you take your shoes off
꽉 차다 = packed full; a constant complaint for shoe lovers
on top of the shoe cabinet
the flat top is a handy drop spot for keys, masks and deliveries
examples: 신발은 신발장에 넣어 주세요.
Please put your shoes in the shoe cabinet.
Polite request to a guest; 넣다 + 에 = 'put into' a place
신발장이 꽉 차서 새 운동화 둘 데가 없어요.
The shoe cabinet is full, so there's nowhere to put my new sneakers.
둘 데가 없다 ('no place to keep it') is a very natural everyday grumble
택배는 신발장 위에 올려 두시면 돼요.
You can just leave the parcel on top of the shoe cabinet.
위에 올려 두다 = 'set on top and leave'; a typical instruction to a courier
nuance: 신발장 is 신발 ('shoes') + 장 (the native-reading of the hanja 欌, 'cabinet/wardrobe') — the same 장 you see in 옷장, 책장, 거실장, so once you learn it you can decode a whole family of furniture words. It sits at the 현관 (entryway) and is bound up with the absolute Korean rule that shoes come off the instant you step inside and go straight in. The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 신발 박스 / 신발 상자, but a 박스/상자 is a cardboard box you'd carry a single pair in — the built-in furniture piece is always 신발장. A second trap is thinking the shoe-removal is optional; saying 신발장에 넣어 주세요 to a guest is itself a polite way of signalling 'shoes off, please'. It collocates with 넣다, 꽉 차다, and 위에 올려 두다.

mistakes: Calling it 신발 박스 or 신발 상자. WHY: 박스/상자 is a cardboard box, not the entryway furniture. FIX: use 신발장 for the built-in cabinet.
Walking in without using it. WHY: the cultural norm is shoes off and into the 신발장 at the door. FIX: take shoes off at the 현관 and place them in the 신발장.
Mixing up the 장 ('cabinet') in 신발장 with 장 ('market', 場/장). WHY: same syllable, different word. FIX: read the 장 in furniture words as 'cabinet' (欌), as in 옷장 and 책장.

usage: a single flat board fixed to a wall or inside a cabinet to set things on
to set up on a shelf
올려 두다 = to place up and leave; the typical 'put it on the shelf' action
달다 = to mount/install; what you do with a drill, bracket, or adhesive
벽 (wall, 壁) + 선반; the wall-mounted type prized in tiny flats to save floor space
examples: 책은 선반에 올려 두세요.
Just set the books on the shelf.
올려 두다 = 'place on top and leave it'; the default verb for putting things on a shelf
화장실에 선반 하나 달았더니 훨씬 깔끔해졌어요.
After I put up one shelf in the bathroom, it got much tidier.
-았더니 reports the result you observed after doing something — common for a small home upgrade
선반이 높아서 발판 없이는 손이 안 닿아요.
The shelf is so high I can't reach it without a step stool.
손이 안 닿다 ('the hand doesn't reach') is the set everyday phrase for 'can't reach'
nuance: 선반 is one single flat shelf board — a ledge — not a whole storage unit. The synonym contrast learners most need: 선반 is one board, whereas 책장 is a standing bookcase (a piece of furniture with many shelves), and 선반 is also not a 서랍 (a pull-out drawer): a 선반 is open and you set things on top, a 서랍 slides out and you put things inside. Note the verb pairing — you 달다 ('mount/install') a 선반 onto a wall, not 만들다, and you 올려 두다 things onto it. In cramped officetels and 원룸, wall-mounted 선반 are a go-to space saver sold cheaply at 다이소 and IKEA, used for kitchen, bathroom and entryway storage alike. The English-speaker pitfall is using 선반 for a full 'bookshelf' unit — in English 'shelf' and 'bookshelf' blur, but in Korean the unit is 책장 and only the board is 선반.

Confusing 선반 (shelf) with 서랍 (drawer). WHY: a 선반 is open and you put things on it; a 서랍 slides out and you put things in it. FIX: 선반 = open ledge, 서랍 = pull-out drawer.
Saying 선반을 만들다 for installing one. WHY: the natural verb for mounting a shelf is 달다. FIX: use 선반을 달다 ('put up / install a shelf').

usage: 거실 居室 (living room) + 장 欌 (cabinet); the long low unit the TV sits on
to set on top of the TV stand
올려놓다 = to place on top; where the TV and remote usually go
장만하다 = to acquire (a sizeable purchase); natural for buying furniture
거실장 typically has drawers for remotes, cables, and odds and ends
examples: 티비는 거실장 위에 있어요.
The TV is on top of the living-room cabinet.
Basic location sentence; 티비 is the casual everyday word for TV
이사하면서 거실장을 하나 장만했어요.
When I moved, I got myself a TV stand.
장만하다 carries a 'finally acquired something substantial' feel that 사다 lacks
리모컨은 거실장 서랍 안에 있을 거예요.
The remote's probably in the drawer of the TV stand.
-(으)ㄹ 거예요 makes it a guess; 서랍 안에 = 'inside the drawer'
nuance: 거실장 is 거실 (living room, Sino-Korean 居室 'dwelling-room') + 장 (cabinet, 欌) — the low, wide cabinet that anchors a Korean living room, with the TV on top and remotes, cables and clutter hidden in its drawers and doors. The key contrast for learners is 거실장 vs 거실: 거실장 is the furniture, 거실 is the room itself — same first two syllables, different things. The English-speaker pitfall is inventing 티비 책상 or 티비 테이블 by direct translation of 'TV table' — those aren't the standard term; native speakers say 거실장 (and informally 티비 다이, from Japanese-via-loan 'dai'). It's one of the first large pieces people buy or inherit when furnishing a home, so it surfaces constantly in moving and shopping talk, where it pairs with 장만하다 ('acquire') and 위에 올려놓다.

Confusing 거실장 with 거실. WHY: 거실장 is the cabinet, 거실 is the living room. FIX: add 장 only when you mean the furniture piece.
Using 사다 where 장만하다 fits better. WHY: for a notable furniture purchase, 장만하다 sounds more natural and warmer. FIX: 거실장을 장만했어요 for 'I got myself a TV stand'.

usage: 화장 化粧 (makeup) + 대 臺 (stand/table); the mirrored table for getting ready
앞에 앉다 = sit in front of; where you do makeup or skincare
거울 (mirror) is the defining feature that makes a table a 화장대
정리 整理 = sorting out; cosmetics pile up, so this is a regular chore
examples: 화장대 거울이 정말 커요.
The vanity mirror is really big.
Simple description; 거울 is the part that defines the piece
화장품이 많아서 화장대가 항상 지저분해요.
I have so much makeup that my vanity is always messy.
지저분하다 = cluttered/messy; the natural adjective for a crowded surface
원룸이라 화장대 놓을 자리가 없어서 그냥 거울만 붙였어요.
Since it's a one-room, there's no space for a vanity, so I just stuck a mirror up.
놓을 자리가 없다 ('no place to set it') captures small-apartment reality
nuance: 화장대 breaks down as 화장 化粧 ('makeup', literally 'transform-adorn') + 대 臺 ('stand/platform'), so it is the dedicated mirrored table where you do makeup and skincare. The dangerous near-twin is 화장실: both start with 화장 化粧, but 화장대 is the dressing table while 화장실 化粧室 is the bathroom/toilet — confusing them in front of a host is a real and embarrassing mix-up. Also keep it apart from 책상 (a work desk): a makeup table specifically is a 화장대, and the 거울 is what distinguishes the two. In small Korean flats it's a coveted but space-hungry item, so many renters skip it for a wall mirror — hence 화장대 놓을 자리가 없다 is a stock phrase. The word signals 'getting-ready space' generally and isn't gendered: men use 화장대 for grooming setups too. It collocates with 거울, 정리, and 앞에 앉다.

Calling it 책상 (desk). WHY: a 책상 is for studying/working; the mirrored makeup table is a 화장대. FIX: use 화장대 when there's a mirror for getting ready.
Assuming it's women-only. WHY: 화장대 just means a grooming table, used by anyone. FIX: it's fine to say a man has a 화장대.

usage: 옷 (clothes) + 걸이 (a thing to hang on, from 걸다); both the small hanger and a standing rack
걸다 = to hang; the core verb built right into the word 옷걸이
a useful request at a store, hotel, or to a roommate
스탠드 (stand) + 옷걸이; the freestanding pole type common in 원룸
examples: 코트는 옷걸이에 거세요.
Hang your coat on the hanger.
거세요 is the polite form of 걸다 ('hang'); 에 marks where you hang it
옷걸이가 모자라서 옷이 자꾸 쌓여요.
I don't have enough hangers, so clothes keep piling up.
모자라다 = to fall short / be insufficient; an everyday frustration
원룸엔 붙박이장이 없어서 스탠드 옷걸이 하나 샀어요.
My one-room has no built-in closet, so I bought a standing coat rack.
ties to 붙박이장; the classic renter workaround when there's no closet
nuance: 옷걸이 is a transparent native compound: 옷 ('clothes') + 걸이, a noun made from the verb 걸다 ('to hang') plus the thing-noun suffix -이 — so it literally means 'the clothes-hanging thing'. That single word covers both the individual coat hanger and a standing or wall-mounted coat rack; context tells you which (스탠드 옷걸이 forces the 'rack' reading). The synonym to separate it from is 옷장: 옷걸이 is the open hanging tool/rack, while 옷장 is the closed cabinet/wardrobe you shut the doors on. The English-speaker pitfall is treating the act and the object as the same — 옷 걸기 (or 옷을 거는 것) is the act of hanging clothes, but the object is 옷걸이; don't say 옷 걸기 when you want the hanger. Because compact rentals often lack a proper 옷장 or 붙박이장, a 스탠드 옷걸이 is the default. It's an everyday word at home, in shops, and in hotels, pairing with 걸다, 모자라다, and 하나 주세요.

Saying 옷 걸기 for the object. WHY: 걸기 names the action of hanging, not the thing. FIX: the noun is 옷걸이.

Reaching for 행거 only. WHY: 행거 ('hanger', a loanword) usually means the big rolling clothes rack, while the plain hanger and pole rack are 옷걸이 / 스탠드 옷걸이. FIX: default to 옷걸이 unless you specifically mean the large rolling rail.

usage: 붙박이 (a fixed/built-in thing, from 붙박다) + 장 欌 (cabinet); a wardrobe fixed into the wall
a major plus when renting; it removes the need to buy an 옷장
to put into the built-in closet
where you stash seasonal clothes, bedding, and suitcases
옵션 (option) = a built-in feature agents list as a selling point
examples: 이 집은 붙박이장이 있어요.
This place has a built-in closet.
A plain 'it has X' selling point; 있다 = to exist/have
붙박이장이 커서 이불이랑 캐리어까지 다 들어가요.
The built-in closet is big, so even the bedding and the suitcase fit inside.
ties to 이불; -까지 ('even') stresses how much it holds
전에 살던 집은 붙박이장이 없어서 너무 불편했어요.
My previous place had no built-in closet, so it was really inconvenient.
전에 살던 집 = 'the place I used to live'; the natural way to compare past housing
nuance: 붙박이장 is 붙박이 + 장 (cabinet, 欌). 붙박이 comes from the verb 붙박다 ('to fix firmly in place'), so the word literally means a 'fixed-in-place cabinet' — a wall-mounted, immovable wardrobe that comes with the apartment. That immovability is the whole point and the key contrast with 옷장: an 옷장 is a free-standing wardrobe you buy and can move out with you, whereas a 붙박이장 is structurally attached and stays. For renters it's hugely practical because it removes the cost and hassle of buying and hauling an 옷장. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 붙박이장 as movable furniture — by definition it isn't; if you can carry it out, it's an 옷장, not a 붙박이장. The other trap is spelling: keep the ㅌ and the double structure — it's 붙박이장, not 붓박이장 or 붙바기장. Real-estate listings flag it as a prized 옵션, so you'll hear it constantly while flat-hunting, alongside 있다 and -까지 다 들어가다.

Misspelling it 붓박이장 or 붙바기장. WHY: it derives from 붙박다, keeping the ㅌ patchim. FIX: the correct spelling is 붙박이장.
Confusing 붙박이장 with 신발장. WHY: both end in 장 but one holds clothes (in the room) and one holds shoes (at the 현관). FIX: 옷 → 붙박이장/옷장; 신발 → 신발장.

usage: the head pillow you sleep on; correctly spelled 베개, not 배개
to rest your head on a pillow
베다 is the dedicated verb; 베개 literally is 'the thing you 베다 on'
커버 (cover); the washable cloth case you launder regularly
height and firmness are what people care about most
examples: 베개가 너무 높아요.
The pillow is too high.
Simple 'too X' description; 높다 ('high') is the usual pillow gripe
새 베개로 바꿨더니 잠이 훨씬 잘 와요.
After I switched to a new pillow, I sleep much better.
잠이 잘 오다 ('sleep comes well') is the idiomatic way to say you fall asleep easily
베개 커버는 일주일에 한 번씩 빨아요.
I wash the pillowcase once a week.
일주일에 한 번씩 = 'once per week each'; 에 marks the time unit for frequency
nuance: 베개 is specifically the pillow you sleep on, and it comes paired with its own unique verb 베다 ('to lay your head on something') — 베개 is essentially 'the thing you 베다 on', so 베개를 베다 ('to pillow your head') is the set collocation, not 베개를 쓰다. Koreans care a lot about a pillow's 높이 (height) and firmness, which spawns follow-up words like 목베개 ('neck pillow') and 메모리폼 ('memory foam'). The biggest English-speaker pitfall is spelling: it is 베개 (tied to the verb 베다), not the very commonly mis-typed 배개 — the ㅔ/ㅐ contrast is easy to get wrong by ear. The second pitfall is meaning: 베개 is only the sleeping pillow; a decorative throw pillow on a sofa is a 쿠션, and a sit-on floor cushion is a 방석. It collocates with 베다, 커버, and 높다.

usage: the main bed covering you sleep under; covers comforters and floor-bedding alike
to pull the blanket over yourself
덮다 = to cover; the verb that pairs with 이불 when you go to sleep
개다 = to fold; a morning habit, especially with floor bedding
bulky wash you often take to a coin laundromat (빨래방)
examples: 이불 덮고 자.
Cover yourself with the blanket and sleep.
Casual 반말 command to family/a friend; 덮다 is the verb for pulling covers over you
겨울 이불은 너무 두꺼워서 세탁기에 안 들어가요.
The winter duvet is so thick it won't fit in the washing machine.
links to 다용도실/세탁기; 안 들어가다 = 'doesn't go in / won't fit'
주말마다 이불 빨아서 햇볕에 말려요.
Every weekend I wash the bedding and dry it in the sun.
햇볕에 말리다 = 'sun-dry'; a common habit out on the 베란다
nuance: 이불 is the all-purpose native word for the blanket / duvet / comforter you sleep under — crucially, it works whether you sleep on a bed or lay bedding directly on the heated floor (the whole floor-bedding set is 이부자리). Its dedicated verb is 덮다 ('to cover'): you 이불을 덮다 to go to sleep and 이불을 개다 ('fold') in the morning. The synonym to separate it from is 담요: a 담요 is a small lap/throw blanket (the thing you drape over your knees), while the main bed covering is 이불 — don't use 담요 for the whole duvet. Also keep 이불 (the covering) apart from 베개 (pillow) and 침대 (bed); 이불 is only what you pull over yourself. The word is bound to seasonal swaps (여름 이불 vs 겨울 이불) and to the chore of washing bulky bedding, which often means a trip to a 빨래방; a thin summer one is a 홑이불. It collocates with 덮다, 개다, and 빨래.

Saying 이불을 쓰다 for going to sleep under it. WHY: the natural verb is 덮다 ('cover'). FIX: use 이불을 덮다.

usage: 방석 方席 (square + seat/mat); the flat cushion you sit on, on the floor or a hard chair
깔다 = to spread/lay down; what you do before sitting on the floor
앉다 = to sit; the natural pair verb for 방석
모자라다 = to run short; a realistic worry when guests come over
examples: 방석에 앉으세요.
Please sit on the cushion.
Polite seating offer; 에 앉다 = 'sit on/at' a spot
의자가 딱딱해서 방석을 깔았어요.
The chair was hard, so I put a cushion on it.
딱딱하다 = hard; 깔다 ('lay down') also covers padding a hard chair
손님 오면 방석이 모자랄 것 같아요.
When guests come, I think we'll be short on cushions.
모자라다 = to run short; -ㄹ 것 같다 softens it to a prediction
nuance: 방석 is Sino-Korean 方席 — 方 ('square') + 席 ('seat/mat') — literally a 'square sitting mat', the flat sit-on cushion central to Korea's floor-sitting (좌식) culture; you'll see stacks of them at floor-seating restaurants, set out for guests, and laid on hard dining chairs. Its verbs are 깔다 ('lay it out') and 앉다 ('sit on it'). The crucial contrast is with 쿠션 and 베개: a 쿠션 is a soft decorative/back cushion you lean against, a 베개 is the pillow you sleep on, and a 방석 is the firm flat one you sit on — three different cushions, three different words. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: don't lump them all under 'cushion', and don't be misled by the spelling into linking 방석 to 방 ('room', 房) — the 방 here is 方 ('square'), unrelated to rooms. Pulling out a 방석 for a visitor is a small but genuine act of hospitality. It collocates with 깔다, 앉다, and 모자라다.

Linking 방석 to 방 ('room'). WHY: the 방 in 방석 is 方 ('square'), not 房 ('room'). FIX: read 방석 as 'square seat-mat', a seating item.
Saying 방석을 놓다 only. WHY: the idiomatic verb for setting one out to sit on is 깔다 ('spread/lay down'). FIX: use 방석을 깔다.

usage: loanword from English 'mattress'; the padded sleeping surface itself
푹신하다 = soft and cushiony; firmness is the main buying factor
만 (only); renters often skip the frame and buy this alone
옮기다 = to move/shift; it's heavy and awkward, especially on moving day
examples: 매트리스가 푹신해요.
The mattress is soft.
Plain description; 푹신하다 is the go-to adjective for a plush mattress
매트리스가 너무 딱딱해서 허리가 배겨요.
The mattress is so firm my back gets sore.
배기다 = (a hard surface) digs into you; the natural complaint about firm bedding
저는 프레임 없이 매트리스만 바닥에 깔고 자요.
I sleep with just a mattress on the floor, no frame.
프레임 없이 = 'without a frame'; a very common budget / one-room setup
nuance: 매트리스 is a straight loanword (외래어) from English 'mattress', and it refers to the padded sleeping pad alone — which is exactly where the synonym contrast bites: 침대 is the whole bed (frame + mattress together), while 매트리스 is only the pad on top. This matters in real life because many Korean renters deliberately buy a 매트리스 by itself and put it straight on the floor or a low platform, skipping a full 침대 frame to save money and space — so 침대 사다 and 매트리스만 사다 describe genuinely different purchases. The everyday talk around it is firmness: 딱딱하다 ('firm/hard') vs 푹신하다 ('plush/soft'), plus the verb 배기다 for when a hard surface digs into your back. The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) saying 침대 when you mean only the mattress, and (2) the loanword spelling — it's 매트리스, not 매트레스 or 메트리스. It collocates with 푹신하다, 딱딱하다, and 옮기다.
